Both articles highlight the utility of Bayesian inference, a method developed by 18th-century minister Thomas Bayes, which allows searchers to calculate probability distributions for a target's location. This method functions by taking initial estimates and continuously updating them as new information—such as radar data, ocean currents, or flight path details—becomes available. A critical feature of this approach is its ability to incorporate negative data; specifically, it lowers the probability that an object is in an area that has already been thoroughly searched without result.

The success of this mathematical approach is illustrated through the case of Air France Flight 447, which disappeared over the Atlantic in 2009. While initial search efforts failed, statisticians from Metron Scientific Solutions were eventually consulted. They utilized Bayesian methods to map probabilities across a grid, accounting for various crash theories and the failure of previous searches to detect the plane’s black box signals. A pivotal moment came when the team adjusted their assumptions to consider the possibility that the black box beacons had failed. This revision shifted the area of highest probability, leading search teams directly to the wreckage on the ocean floor in 2011.

Regarding Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, the articles suggest that Bayesian methods are theoretically well-suited for the task but face significant challenges. The disappearance involves complex variables, including the possibility of deliberate diversion, which drastically alters probability landscapes. While advocates argue that the method brings necessary discipline to the search process, some statisticians caution that the drastic and conflicting nature of the evidence in the MH370 case may limit the model's effectiveness. Furthermore, there is uncertainty regarding whether the Malaysian authorities have employed these rigorous statistical techniques to the same degree as the French investigators did previously. Ultimately, while Bayesian statistics offer a powerful framework for refining search areas, experts warn that without breakthrough data, the vastness of the Indian Ocean may keep Flight 370 hidden. reference_answer: Forget satellite images and aerial searches—the best way to find Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 may be with mathematical techniques dating back to the 18th century, the BBC reports. That's how Air France flight 447 was found in 2009, using "Bayesian statistics" to measure the probability of the plane being in one place or another. Named after Presbyterian minister and mathematician Thomas Bayes, the technique allowed experts to apply several factors to each point on a map: For example, what was the chance it crashed from mechanical failure? How far do planes tend to crash from their last known location? What was the chance that search teams missed debris in various locations? It's like picking a restaurant by balancing how full it is, what your favorite restaurant-review website says, and so on—except that experts hunting for Airbus A330 did that for each point where plane may have crashed in the Atlantic, Five Thirty-Eight notes. It was so hard that the US team of statisticians invited by France gave up, until they de-emphasized one statistic: that a plane's black box emits a signal after a crash 90% of the time. They changed their findings, and presto, the plane was found. Bayesian techniques have helped people find World War II U-boats, men overboard, and sunken treasure, but there's no evidence that Malaysia is employing them now. "I suspect that they just guess, like professional baseball managers used to do before Moneyball," says a biostatistician.
